title: Log-Based Streaming
summary: Kafka's commit-log model — partitions, consumer groups, and offsets as a replayable source of truth instead of a disappearing queue.

slides.markdown:
Kafka and similar systems don't work like a queue where a message disappears once consumed — they work like an append-only log that consumers read through, at their own pace, without deleting anything. That single design choice is why Kafka can replay history, serve dozens of independent readers, and scale to millions of events per second.

This topic covers the mental model: partitions, consumer groups, offsets, and ordering — the vocabulary you need to reason about Kafka in an interview instead of just naming it.

slides.sectionTitle: The commit log model: Kafka as an append-only, replayable log
slides.markdown:
A **commit log** is an append-only sequence of records, each assigned a strictly increasing position. Kafka's core abstraction, the **topic**, is exactly this: producers append records to the end, and nothing already written is ever modified or removed on read.

This is fundamentally different from a queue, where consuming a message typically removes it. In Kafka, reading a record doesn't delete it — the record stays in the log (until retention expires it) and any number of consumers can read the same record independently, each tracking its own position.

That replay-ability is the headline feature: a new consumer can join tomorrow and read the last 7 days of history from the start, something a traditional queue can't offer once a message has been consumed and removed.

slides.sectionTitle: Partitions: how a topic scales horizontally
slides.markdown:
A Kafka topic is split into **partitions** — independent, ordered logs that together make up the topic. Writing spreads across partitions (usually by hashing a key), and reading can happen in parallel, one reader per partition.

A topic with 12 partitions can be consumed by up to 12 parallel readers simultaneously — each owns a slice of the topic, reading its own log independently of the others. Adding partitions is how you raise the topic's maximum parallelism; adding consumers beyond the partition count just leaves the extras idle.

This is the mechanism behind Kafka's throughput: instead of one shared log everyone contends for, you get N independent logs that scale close to linearly with partition count.

slides.sectionTitle: Diagram: topic, partitions, and consumer groups mapped out
slides.markdown:
![A topic split into 4 partitions, each an ordered log, with a 3-consumer group assigned across them so one consumer covers two partitions](assets/partitions-consumer-group.svg)

Each partition is its own ordered append-only log with sequential **offsets**. A consumer group divides the partitions among its members — here, 3 consumers cover 4 partitions, so one consumer is assigned two.

No partition is ever read by two consumers in the *same* group at once — that exclusivity is what makes parallel consumption safe without any locking.

slides.sectionTitle: Consumer groups and offsets: parallelism without losing your place
slides.markdown:
A **consumer group** is a named set of consumers that split a topic's partitions among themselves — each partition assigned to exactly one consumer in the group at a time. An **offset** is a consumer's saved position in a partition: "I've read up through record 48,291."

Because the offset is tracked (usually committed back to Kafka itself), a consumer that crashes and restarts, or gets reassigned a partition after a rebalance, resumes from its last committed offset instead of from the beginning or losing its place.

Two separate consumer groups reading the same topic don't interfere with each other at all: each group tracks its own offsets independently, so a fraud-detection group and an analytics group can both read every record, each at its own pace, without one blocking the other.

slides.sectionTitle: Ordering guarantees: per-partition order, not global order
slides.markdown:
Kafka guarantees order **within a partition**: records written to partition 3 are read back from partition 3 in the exact order they were written. It makes **no** such guarantee across partitions — records in partition 1 and partition 2 have no defined relative order.

This matters for key choice: if you need all events for a given user processed in order, you must route them to the same partition, typically by hashing the user ID as the partition key. Two events for the same user landing on different partitions could be processed out of order.

Interview signal: when someone asks "does Kafka guarantee ordering," the precise answer is "per-partition, if you've chosen your partition key correctly" — not an unqualified yes.

slides.sectionTitle: Compare: a traditional message queue vs a log-based stream
slides.markdown:
| | Traditional queue | Log-based stream (e.g. Kafka) |
|---|---|---|
| Read model | Message removed once consumed | Message stays in the log; any consumer can read it |
| Replay | Not possible once consumed | Replay from any offset, within retention |
| Multiple independent readers | Needs a separate queue per reader group | One log, many consumer groups, no duplication |
| Ordering | Often global, per-queue | Per-partition only |
| Best fit | Task distribution: one worker does the job | Event streaming: many readers, history matters |

**How to decide:** if several independent systems each need to read the same full history of events, or you need to replay the past, reach for a log; if you just need work distributed once to a worker pool, a traditional queue is simpler and sufficient.

slides.sectionTitle: Retention and replay: treating the log as a source of truth
slides.markdown:
Kafka doesn't keep records forever — a **retention** policy (commonly time-based, e.g. 7 days, or size-based) decides when old records are deleted from a partition, independent of whether any consumer has read them.

Because records aren't removed on read, any consumer group can **replay**: reset its offset back to an earlier point and reprocess everything since then. This is what makes it practical to fix a bug in a consumer, roll the offset back a day, and reprocess that day's events with the corrected logic — something a destructive queue can't offer once messages are gone.

Some systems push this further and treat the log itself as the durable source of truth, rebuilding downstream databases or caches entirely by replaying it from the start — a compacted topic, keeping only the latest value per key, is the usual way to make that replay bounded in size.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: picking a partition key that skews load onto one partition
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "I'll just partition by a convenient field, like `event_type` — there are only 4 event types anyway."

**Why it's wrong:** with only 4 distinct keys, all traffic for the most common event type piles onto one partition, no matter how many partitions the topic has — that partition becomes a bottleneck no amount of extra partitions or consumers can relieve, since one consumer can only handle one partition at a time.

**Correct model:** pick a partition key with enough distinct, evenly-distributed values to spread load — a user ID or order ID typically works far better than a low-cardinality field like event type or status.
